Reflection Principle

ProbabilityCountingSequences
Game: A walker takes up-and-down steps from A to B. A second walker starts at the mirror point A' and copies the first one backwards until it reaches the middle line. There is nothing to win — compare the two paths.
How to play: Move the sliders to choose the start, finish and number of steps. Press One walk to see both paths; tick Show names to label A, A' and B.

Look for the math

Counting walks is hard when you add a condition such as "must touch the axis". The reflection trick turns those walks into ordinary walks, which are much easier to count.

The two walks

Each step goes one place right and one place up or down. The purple walk starts at A = (0, a) above the axis. The green one starts at its mirror image A' = (0, −a). Until the green walk touches the axis it takes the opposite step from the purple one; after that it copies the purple walk step for step. Press One walk until the two lines overlap.

Why the pairing works

Take a purple walk that touches the axis, and let its first touch be at step k. Reflect the first k steps in the axis; leave the rest alone. The new walk starts at A' and ends at B. Conversely, every walk from A' to B must cross the axis, so reflecting its first part gives back a unique touching walk from A.

Counting them

Write Nn(a, b) for all walks from (0,a) to (n,b) and Mn(a, b) for those that touch or cross the axis. The pairing gives Mn(a, b) = Nn(−a, b) for positive a and b. The number on the right is a binomial coefficient: with u = (n + b + a)/2 up-steps, it is C(n, u). If n and b − a have different parity, the applet quietly uses one fewer step.

What was checked

The test lists every up/down sequence for small lengths and compares the counts with the binomial formula. It writes the applet's two walk rules a second time and checks every step of both paths on seeded walks, and it verifies the touching-walk correspondence by brute force for small positive heights. One quirk is kept: when a = 0 the reflected walk waits for itself to reach zero before copying, so the reflection is not the textbook one; the lemma is only claimed for a > 0.

Set a = 3, b = 4 and n = 9, then press One walk several times until the two paths meet partway across.
